newsitem.title: USA: Murdoch satellite TV deal to get close U.S. scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch satellite TV deal to get close U.S. scrutiny.

text.p: Rupert Murdoch is likely to be grilled by government officials over teaming up with cable television operators to offer satellite TV only weeks after vowing to fight the cable industry with a now-defunct satellite venture.

A U.S. official said Wednesday regulators will pore over the deal between Murdoch's News Corp. and PrimeStar Partners -- a satellite TV service owned by the biggest cable players -- to see its impact on competition in cable and satellite television.
"It will get close scrutiny," said Peter Cowhey, head of the Federal Communications Commission's international bureau. "It's a major development in the market."
Consumer advocates and others already are criticising the venture, calling it yet another deal that violates the spirit of competition envisioned by last year's communications law.
"There's a very good chance that citizens groups will oppose the deal before the FCC and also on antitrust grounds," said Andrew Schwartzman of the Media Access Project.
Aside from the FCC, antitrust enforcers at the Justice Department or the Federal Trade Commission will review the transaction. And the deal is raising concern on Capitol Hill.
"Congress and the American public will not put up with an unregulated monopoly," said Representative W.J. (Billy) Tauzin, R-La.

"We're either going to have real competition out there -- where consumers have real choices and are not bound by programming they don't want and aren't bound to pay any price the controlling interests demand -- or we're going to end up with not only continued, but intensified, regulation."

Murdoch's News Corp. will gain entry to the U.S. satellite TV market through a restructuring of PrimeStar. PrimeStar will become a public company and include satellites contolled by News Corp. and satellite TV partner MCI Communications Corp.

In exchange for the satellites, News Corp and MCI will get a non-voting stake in the new PrimeStar Inc. of no more than 20 percent -- a level below the 25 percent cap on foreign investments by companies like Australia-based News Corp.
The deal follows News Corp.'s failed bid to join with EchoStar Communications Corp. in a $1 billion satellite broadcast venture Murdoch said would challenge cable TV.

Direct satellite broadcast (DBS) operators like EchoStar -- whose customers get the high-quality digital service over a pizza-sized dish -- have about 5 million subscribers and are fighting to attract some of cable's 65 million viewers.
Murdoch in April asked lawmakers to change the copyright laws so his venture with EchoStar -- now engulfed in litigation -- could compete with cable.
"If you give us the legal authority to compete, the rest is up to us," he told the Senate Commerce Committee.
PrimeStar currently has 1.8 million satellite subscribers. The addition of the News Corp.-MCI satellites will give it the ability to compete in the fast-growing DBS market.
Murdoch will be teaming up with the biggest names in cable. PrimeStar owners include: Tele-Communications Inc. (TCI), Time Warner Inc., and Comcast Corp.
The FCC's Cowhey said his agency will look at:
-- The impact on channel capacity for satellites used to beam TV programmes around the nation.
-- The impact on competition between providers of cable TV, high-powered DBS TV, and direct-to-home (DTH) satellite TV that must use larger dishes than DBS.
-- The impact on other DBS providers' access to programmes such as those distributed by News Corp.'s Fox TV network.
-- The impact on the three orbital satellite slots now capable of beaming programmes nationwide. News Corp and MCI will contribute one of the three slots in the new venture.
A unit of Tele-Communications, which is involved in PrimeStar, now shares one of the other two slots with EchoStar.

PrimeStar has agreed to sell the rights to the slot and occupy the more attractive one bought by MCI at an FCC airwave auction. "The deal was structured so that antitrust concerns will not preclude it," said News Corp. lobbyist Peggy Binzel.
